nameStory: The 'scarlet' in scarlet toothcup refers to the deep red coloration that often develops in the leaves and stems, especially as the plant matures. The 'toothcup' name comes from the tiny, tooth-like sepals that form a small cup around the base of each delicate flower.
description: Scarlet toothcup is a small annual wildflower that's quite rare in New England, being far outside its typical range. This low-growing plant reaches up to three feet tall when upright, though it often sprawls along the ground instead. Its narrow leaves can range from green to striking deep red, and it produces clusters of tiny rose to lavender flowers with bright yellow centers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, linear leaves up to 3 inches long that feel smooth and slightly succulent. They often develop beautiful deep red or burgundy coloration, especially on the stems and leaf edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny rounded flowers in clusters of 3-5 in the leaf joints along the upper stem. Rose to lavender petals are just a few millimeters long with bright yellow stamens that stick out noticeably.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Annual herb that may grow upright to nearly 3 feet or sprawl along wet ground. Stems are often reddish and feel somewhat fleshy to the touch.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, rounded seed capsules about 1/4 inch wide that split open to release many tiny seeds. The capsules feel papery when mature.

habitat: In its native range, scarlet toothcup thrives in consistently moist areas like pond edges, riverbanks, and wet meadows. If found in New England, it would likely be in similar wetland habitats, possibly as a rare introduction or garden escape near water features.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms. Young plants emerge as small green shoots with narrow leaves.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs through summer months. This is the best time for identification when the characteristic tiny clustered flowers are visible.
seasonality.fall: Fruits mature and plants often develop their most intense red coloration. Seeds are dispersed before first frost kills the annual plant.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as this annual dies completely, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil.

funFact: Despite being called 'scarlet toothcup,' this plant is so rare in New England that it's been recorded only once in the entire region - making any sighting a truly exceptional botanical discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups!
confusionNotes: The narrow leaves and wet habitat might cause confusion with young water willows or other wetland plants, but scarlet toothcup's tiny clustered flowers with protruding yellow stamens and the reddish coloration of mature plants are distinctive. Remember: if the flowers are bigger than your pinky nail, it's probably not toothcup.
contextualKnowledge: Scarlet toothcup belongs to the loosestrife family, but don't confuse it with the infamous invasive purple loosestrife - they're distant relatives with very different appearances. This plant is native to most of the US but naturally absent from New England, so any sighting here would be botanically noteworthy.
compareHints: Since scarlet toothcup is the only Ammannia species in our region, compare it to other small wetland plants in the loosestrife family. Unlike purple loosestrife with its tall spikes of large purple flowers, toothcup has tiny flowers in small clusters. Unlike swamp loosestrife, toothcup's leaves are much narrower and often reddish.
